trial_name: Annane 2002 — Low-Dose Hydrocortisone and Fludrocortisone in Septic Shock
citation: Annane D, Sébille V, Charpentier C, Bollaert P-E, François B, Korach J-M, et al. Effect of treatment with low doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone on mortality in patients with septic shock. JAMA. 2002;288(7):862-871.
one_liner: 7-day low-dose hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality and accelerated vasopressor withdrawal in corticotropin nonresponders with early, severe septic shock.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with early catecholamine-dependent septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation
pico.intervention: Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h (200 mg/day) plus fludrocortisone 50 µg enterally q24h for 7 days
pico.comparison: Matched IV placebo q6h plus matched enteral placebo q24h for 7 days
pico.outcome: 28-day survival distribution in corticotropin nonresponders (serum cortisol increase <= 9 µg/dL after 250 µg corticotropin)

background.existing_knowledge: Earlier high-dose corticosteroid strategies in sepsis failed to improve survival and raised safety concerns.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether physiologic stress-dose hydrocortisone and mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) accelerate shock reversal and improve survival in septic shock patients with relative adrenal insufficiency.
background.hypothesis: 7-day replacement therapy with hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone improves 28-day survival distribution in early catecholamine-dependent septic shock patients with impaired adrenal responsiveness to corticotropin.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial in 19 adult ICUs in France; enrolment April 1995 to March 1999; randomisation stratified by centre (block size 4).
methods.setting: 19 adult ICUs in France; 100% of patients mechanically ventilated at inclusion.

inclusion: Adults in ICU with suspected or proven infection and systemic inflammatory response
Hypotension and vasopressor dependence for >= 1 hour (dopamine >= 15 µg/kg/min, or epinephrine/norepinephrine > 0.2 µg/kg/min)
Randomisation within 3 hours of shock onset (amended to <= 8 hours)
exclusion: Recent use of ketoconazole, rifampin, phenytoin, or phenobarbital

methods.intervention: Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours (200 mg/day) plus fludrocortisone 50 µg enterally once daily for 7 days.
methods.comparison: Matched IV placebo every 6 hours plus matched enteral placebo once daily for 7 days.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors) using matched IV and enteral placebos in sequentially numbered boxes.
methods.sample_size_power: 270 patients planned to detect a 20% absolute difference in 28-day mortality in corticotropin nonresponders (assumed 95% placebo nonresponder mortality, 40% nonresponder prevalence) with 90% power and one-sided alpha 0.05. Two interim analyses planned using O'Brien-Fleming stopping boundaries.
methods.primary_outcome: 28-day survival distribution in corticotropin nonresponders (defined by a serum cortisol increase <= 9 µg/dL 30/60 minutes after 250 µg IV tetracosactrin).
methods.follow_up: 28 days (primary endpoint), ICU discharge, hospital discharge, and 1 year.

headline_bullets: 28-day survival distribution significantly improved with corticosteroids in corticotropin nonresponders (53% vs 63% mortality; HR 0.67; P=0.02).
Vasopressor withdrawal was significantly faster with steroids in nonresponders (median 7 vs 10 days; HR 1.91; P=0.001).
No mortality benefit was observed among corticotropin responders (28-day mortality 61% vs 53%; P=0.96).
Predefined steroid-attributable adverse event rates were similar between groups (21% vs 22%; P=0.89).

outcomes_table.note: Pre-specified analysis in nonresponders (cortisol rise <= 9 µg/dL)

safety: Composite steroid-attributable adverse events: 32/150 (21%) in steroid group vs 33/149 (22%) in placebo group (P=0.89)
Superinfection: 12% in steroid group vs 13% in placebo group
Gastrointestinal bleeding: 7% in steroid group vs 5% in placebo group
Psychiatric disorders: 2% in steroid group vs 5% in placebo group
Wound infection: 0/150 (0%) in steroid group vs 7/149 (5%) in placebo group (P=0.007)

domains.notes: Central randomization stratified by centre with block size of 4; sequentially numbered boxes preserved allocation concealment.
Double-blind using indistinguishable matched IV and enteral placebos.
300 randomized; 1 post-randomization consent withdrawal excluded; 299 analyzed ITT. 1 patient died before drug administration but was included in analysis.
Near-complete study drug adherence (150/150 steroid group, 148/149 placebo group received study drug). Open-label crossover not reported.

Well balanced: SAPS II 57±18 vs 60±18; LOD score 7.8±3.1 vs 7.9±2.7; arterial lactate 4.3±3.4 vs 4.6±3.0 mmol/L; time from shock to vasopressors 3.5±2.2 vs 3.7±2.2 h; time on vasopressors before study drug 4.1±3.0 vs 4.1±2.4 h; appropriate antibiotic administration 91% vs 95% (time to appropriate antibiotics 7.1±10.4 vs 6.0±7.3 h).

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong given double-blind placebo control, central concealed allocation, objective primary endpoints, and high protocol adherence.

domains.notes: High severity of illness ( universal mechanical ventilation, catecholamine dependence, high mortality), representing a severe septic shock phenotype.
Excluded recent steroid and etomidate use; conducted 1995–1999 prior to modern resuscitation bundles and low tidal volume ventilation.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate: findings apply to high-acuity, vasopressor-dependent septic shock, though modern practice care bundles differ from the study era.

strengths: Early intervention in severe, catecholamine-dependent shock
Pre-specified biological subgroup analysis based on corticotropin response
Objective survival and hemodynamics endpoints with 1-year follow-up
limitations: Primary inference relies on corticotropin nonresponse subgroup, which was unexpectedly prevalent (~76–77%)
Power calculation assumed a one-sided alpha of 0.05 and a very high placebo mortality (95%)
Small responder subgroup size limits precision for that cohort
Co-interventions and open-label steroid crossovers were not fully reported

critical_appraisal.summary: Landmark trial demonstrating that low-dose hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduces mortality and duration of vasopressor support in corticotropin nonresponders with severe septic shock.
strengths: Concealed central allocation and complete blinding
Clear separation in time to vasopressor withdrawal
weaknesses: Conducted prior to modern sepsis bundle standardization

sections.authors_conclusion: A 7-day treatment with low doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone significantly reduces the risk of death in patients with septic shock and relative adrenal insufficiency without increasing adverse events.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Low-dose corticosteroids accelerate shock reversal and improve survival in severe septic shock.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with early, catecholamine-dependent septic shock requiring moderate-to-high dose vasopressors.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Corticotropin stimulation testing is required before initiating corticosteroid therapy in clinical practice.
implementation_caveats: Current guidelines recommend IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for septic shock refractory to vasopressors without routine ACTH testing.
The addition of enteral fludrocortisone (50 µg daily) remains common when using intermittent hydrocortisone boluses, supported by subsequent trial data (APROCCHSS).

controversies.notes: Annane 2002 suggested benefit was isolated to nonresponders, but subsequent trials (e.g., CORTICUS) showed ACTH response did not reliably predict clinical benefit, leading guidelines to abandon routine ACTH testing.

controversies.topic: Hydrocortisone alone vs combination with fludrocortisone
controversies.notes: Whether enteral fludrocortisone adds meaningful mineralocorticoid effect beyond hydrocortisone's intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity remains actively debated across trials (ADRENAL vs APROCCHSS).

context_related_trials.relation: Evaluated hydrocortisone alone in septic shock; found accelerated shock reversal but no survival benefit, and corticotropin response did not predict treatment effect.
Evaluated continuous hydrocortisone infusion in septic shock; found faster shock resolution and shorter ICU stay, but no difference in 90-day mortality.
Evaluated hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone in severe septic shock; demonstrated improved 90-day survival and increased vasopressor-free days, validating the combination strategy.

unresolved_questions: Does fludrocortisone provide incremental benefit over hydrocortisone alone in septic shock?
Is hydrocortisone bolus administration equivalent to continuous infusion in preventing glycemic variability?

numbers_to_remember: Vasopressor withdrawal in nonresponders: median 7 vs 10 days (HR 1.91, P=0.001)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Stress-dose hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) plus fludrocortisone (50 µg/day) for 7 days accelerates vasopressor withdrawal and reduces mortality in severe septic shock.
